identity.hardware: SPICE module, built from the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF, STS-87) hardware: a fan-driven flow duct (nominally 76 x 76 mm, about 170 mm long) with honeycomb flow straightener, onboard hot-wire anemometer, interchangeable 0.41/0.76/1.6 mm ID burner tubes on the duct axis, 0-500 sccm (N2-equivalent) mass flow controller fed from 12 fuel bottles, hot-wire igniter, retractable ruler, thermopile radiometer, Nikon D100 still camera (top view), colour video camera (front view via mirror) with a data-overlay titler, and a crew control box. The same duct was later reused by BASS, BASS-II and SLICE.

one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station burned tiny gas jets in a gentle, adjustable air stream and turned the fuel up until each flame just started to give off smoke, to learn how air flow and burner size control soot release when there is no gravity.
summary: SPICE measured laminar smoke points, the largest flame that releases no soot, of round gas-jet diffusion flames burning in co-flowing air inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS between February and June 2009. The crew set the air speed with a fan, ignited the flame on a 0.41, 0.76 or 1.6 mm burner and raised the fuel flow until soot escaped the tip; luminous lengths were measured from the downlinked video. About 526 flame conditions were logged and 52-55 smoke points found for ethylene, propane, propylene and 75%/50% propylene in nitrogen, at co-flow speeds of 5.4-65 cm/s. Methane flames reached the end of the duct without smoking. Smoke-point length grew with co-flow speed and with smaller burners, scaling as d^-0.91 u^0.41, and was roughly proportional to fuel mass flow over stoichiometric mixture fraction; a simple residence-time model did not collapse the data. Propane was unusually sooty in microgravity. For spacecraft fire safety the results show that ventilation speed and fuel-jet size, not only fuel type, decide whether a small non-buoyant flame emits smoke.

question.text: Laminar smoke points are a standard measure of how readily a fuel forms soot, and on Earth they are shaped by buoyancy. In a 1988 paper Glassman predicted that non-buoyant flames would not have smoke points at all, but aircraft and Space Shuttle tests (Laminar Soot Processes, LSP, in still air) found them. SPICE asked how smoke points of non-buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames depend on the surrounding air flow (co-flow velocity) and burner diameter, which together control the residence time of soot in the flame. Specific aims: (1) measure non-buoyant smoke points of several gaseous fuels; (2) find the effects of co-flow velocity and burner diameter on smoke points and luminous flame lengths; (3) rank the sooting propensity of the fuels; (4) test flame-shape and residence-time models against the data. The stated hypothesis (30-day report) was that smoke points would be observed in co-flowing flames and would depend on nozzle diameter and co-flow velocity.

physics.text: A gas-jet diffusion flame burns where fuel from the nozzle meets air diffusing in. Soot forms on the fuel-rich side and is normally burnt out as it crosses the flame sheet near the tip. As the fuel flow (and flame length) is raised, the tip cools, largely by soot radiation, until soot oxidation stops and soot escapes: that luminous length is the laminar smoke point. Shorter smoke points mean sootier fuels. In 1 g, buoyancy accelerates the hot gas, so residence time grows only weakly with flow, and soot forms near the flame sheet and moves inward. Without buoyancy, the flow decelerates, residence times are long, and soot forms near the cool core and is carried straight toward the flame sheet. Radiative losses then dominate and the tip can extinguish, giving an 'open-tipped' flame that sheds soot in an annular shell. An imposed co-flow restores some control over residence time: faster air shortens the time soot spends in the formation region and may speed oxygen transport for soot burnout. A smaller nozzle raises the jet exit velocity at the same mass flow. Both are expected to push the smoke point to longer flames. Flame length itself depends mainly on fuel mass flow divided by the stoichiometric mixture fraction, not on nozzle size. Criteria proposed for the smoke point include a tip (soot) temperature of about 1300 K in 1 g and about 1000 K in microgravity, a radiative loss fraction of 0.2-0.4 (1 g) or 0.4-0.6 (0 g), or a luminous length about twice the stoichiometric length.

sources.quote: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet.

apparatus.text: The SPICE module was the reworked Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) apparatus flown in the Shuttle middeck glovebox on STS-87 (1997). It was launched to ISS on ULF-2 in 2008 and run in the MSG at ISS cabin pressure (the MSG runs about 1.3 mbar below cabin). A DC fan drew glovebox air through a ceramic honeycomb and screen into a duct described as about 76 x 76 mm with rounded corners and about 170 mm long. The final report instead gives interior dimensions of 172 x 43 x 43 mm. Air and products left through a perforated copper plate and screen (soot trap) 120 mm downstream of the burner exit. For safety the fan always ran at a minimum of 5.5 V (overlay FAN number 55-139). An onboard TSI 8475 hot-wire anemometer (rated 5-254 cm/s, +/-3% of reading +/-1% of range) near the inlet gave the AIR overlay reading, calibrated on the ground against a probe 13 mm above the burner tip. Three burner tubes (0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm ID) were swapped by the crew. Fuel came from 150 ml bottles through a regulator and a 0-500 sccm (N2-equivalent) mass flow controller set by a potentiometer on the crew control box. A hot-wire (Kanthal) igniter and a retractable 105 mm ruler for length calibration could be swung to the nozzle. An Oriel thermopile radiometer (90 deg view) gave a qualitative radiation signal; it failed its accuracy verification because of EMI susceptibility. Imaging was a Nikon D100 12-bit still camera (3008 x 2000 pixels, 60 mm lens) through the top window and a Panasonic colour video camera viewing the front window via a 45 deg mirror. A titler stamped fuel flow, fan setting, air reading and radiometer gain on the video, logged at 4 Hz.

procedure.text: The safety package planned, per fuel, nine test points (two co-flow levels, 50% and 100% of maximum, times three burners, at 100% and 50% of the smoke-point fuel flow) plus about five repeats: 54 planned flames plus about 30 repeats. In practice the crew set the fan, ignited the flame with the hot wire, then adjusted fuel flow (and in later sessions swept the air speed) to bracket the smoke point. The crew used a cue card: look for the change from a distinct flame tip to dull red/orange breaking through it. Ground staff at the GRC TeleScience Center watched the real-time downlink at the same time. Flames were steady within about 5 s of any change. Typical burns lasted about 60 s, and after every two burns the MSG was flushed with cabin air for 3 minutes. For each condition the crew took a bracketed trio of Nikon stills, and a ruler reference image was taken for scale. Post-flight, smoke-point conditions were picked from the video. L_SP was measured on axis from the burner tip to the point of steepest grayscale change between yellow and black, which spans 2-5 mm. Flow rates were read from the overlay, and pixel-to-mm calibrations were made per day and per video source. Twelve sessions ran from 14 February (GMT 045) to 23 June 2009 (GMT 174). On 15 June (GMT 166) the crew vacuumed soot from the clogged outlet screen. A normal-gravity campaign with the prototype SPICE module and a 13.7 mm unconfined co-flow burner was run at the University of Maryland (Dotson thesis).

psi_data.summary: PSI-107 holds 188 files (6.95 GB); 59 are downloaded locally. Text-bearing documents are readable: the 2011 final report (a draft with editing notes, appendices B-F empty), the 30-day post-flight report with the 2009 Eastern States paper, the 2009 Dotson M.S. thesis, the 2010 AIAA presentation, two crew-training decks, the safety data package, the science verification report, a duct-velocity memo and an image organization guide. The SRD (.doc) and two .ppt decks could not be extracted. The most valuable structured file is 'Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls' (526 rows, 43 columns). For every logged condition it gives GMT times, test number, fuel, nozzle, overlay fuel/air/fan/radiometer readings, converted fuel and air rates, video and Nikon flame lengths and widths, a smoke Y/N flag, and Nikon file IDs. 'SmokePointReview-0g-3.xlsx' lists the 55 microgravity smoke points with derived u_a, u_f, Re, \dot m_f/Z_st and residence-time estimates, plus normal-gravity and shuttle comparison points. The PSI experimental table is a 9-column extract of the master sheet. It drops the measurement columns (flame length, Nikon dimensions, smoke flag, data timestamp) and the GMT 062 methane session, so it holds flow settings only. Raw imagery (NEF zips, jpeg/contact-sheet zips, 83 downlink frame-grab zips, picture-book .ppt, 20 videos; about 6.9 GB) is not downloaded. 22 duct-calibration and 8 fuel-flow-calibration files are present (one of each not downloaded).

findings.claim: Laminar smoke points exist for non-buoyant co-flowing jet flames, contrary to Glassman's 1988 prediction. On the ISS, 52 smoke points (final-report table: 6 ethylene, 6 propane, 20 propylene, 13 for 75% and 7 for 50% propylene; the same report's closing remarks say 55) were found at 0.41-1.6 mm burners and 5.4-65 cm/s co-flow. All smoke-point flames were attached, with Re 36-788.

findings.claim: For a given fuel and burner, raising the co-flow velocity lengthens the smoke point, even though at fixed fuel flow it shortens the luminous flame. Example (pure propylene, 1.6 mm burner, smoke-point review sheet): L_SP rose from about 14.0 mm at u_a = 9.1 cm/s to 25.7 mm at 51.4 cm/s. The investigators attribute this to decreased residence times and radiative losses as co-flow velocity increases.

sources.quote: For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times and radiative losses as coflow velocity increases
Increasing co)flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.

findings.claim: Smaller burners give longer smoke points in co-flow. Propylene smoke points at about 25-27 cm/s co-flow were about 16-18 mm (1.6 mm burner, 22-30 cm/s), 22-23 mm (0.76 mm) and 53 mm (0.41 mm). The step from 0.76 to 0.41 mm is much larger than from 1.6 to 0.76 mm. Extrapolated to zero co-flow the diameter dependence diminishes. The extrapolation matches the earlier still-air shuttle (LSP) smoke points for ethylene; for propane on the 0.76 mm burner it falls at the lower end of the LSP range.

relevance.text: SPICE is fundamental soot science, not a material flammability test. Its main fire-safety value: in microgravity, whether a small flame releases smoke depends strongly on the local ventilation speed and on the size of the fuel source, not just on the fuel. Faster co-flow (5-65 cm/s, spanning typical cabin ventilation) and smaller fuel jets let flames grow longer before smoking. Non-buoyant flames well past their smoke point open at the tip and shed quenched soot, which is also the main carrier of CO and the signal smoke detectors respond to. Propane was relatively sootier in microgravity than its 1 g ranking suggests, so 1 g sooting indices may not transfer directly. The data and correlations (L_SP vs \dot m_f/Z_st, d^-0.91 u^0.41) are benchmarks for soot models used to predict radiation and smoke yield of spacecraft fires. The SPICE duct itself became the platform for BASS solid-fuel flammability and suppression tests and SLICE lifted-flame tests. These are gas-jet results at about 1 atm and 21% O2; they do not give material ignition or spread limits.

sources.quote: Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.

Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities.
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS.

habitat_conditions.text: All SPICE flames burned in ISS cabin air: O2 19-24% (assumed 21 +/- 1%), about 101 kPa, which is close to the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa). Neither O2 nor pressure was varied. The proposed lunar habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less) and suits (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa) are outside the tested range. Higher O2 raises flame temperature and soot formation and lower pressure reduces soot, so SPICE smoke points cannot be applied to those atmospheres without new tests. The co-flow range (5-65 cm/s) does cover realistic ventilation speeds. There is no partial-gravity SPICE data.

sources.quote: The oxygen mole fraction of this cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%.

earth_benefits.text: Smoke points are a classical metric for fuel sooting propensity used in fire modelling and in correlating soot and radiation of turbulent flames (e.g. gas-turbine soot emissions correlate with TSI). Many practical flames are effectively non-buoyant, so SPICE's co-flow data help predict heat release and soot emission in combustors such as jet engines and furnaces. Soot is also a pollutant linked to premature deaths and climate warming.

gaps: DATA ODDITY - 34 duplicate rows in the PSI experimental table: they are not repeated tests. The table is a 9-column extract of 'Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls'. In that sheet each condition usually has a video-measurement row and a Nikon still-image row with identical flow settings, differing only in columns the CSV drops (GMT data timestamp, video vs Nikon flame length, smoke flag, ISS image IDs). Matching the CSV row-for-row to the master (minus GMT 062): the 34 extra rows fall in 31 identical-row groups. 27 groups have distinct data timestamps; the other 4 share a timestamp and pair a video length with a Nikon image record. Two are 'Ku LOS' rows with no data. De-duplicating the CSV would therefore delete real measurement records; they should be tagged video/still instead.

DATA ODDITY - air rate -5.92 cm/s (3 rows, GMT 167, 50% propylene, 0.41 mm burner, ignition time 'LOS'): an artefact, not a reverse flow. The master sheet converts the overlay AIR reading with u_a = 0.9402*AIR - 5.918 (Reference sheet). For these three rows the AIR and FAN cells are blank because the downlink was lost (LOS), so the formula returned its intercept. Treat them as missing. Likewise -0.28 and 0.66 cm/s (6 rows, GMT 136) correspond to AIR readings of 6-7 at the minimum fan setting with a soot-clogged outlet screen, below the anemometer's 5 cm/s rated minimum. They mean 'near-zero, unreliable', not negative flow.

DATA ODDITY - the PSI experimental table omits the whole GMT 062 session (3 March 2009; 57 methane rows in the master sheet: 0.41/0.76/1.6 mm, up to 357 sccm, flames to 110 mm). That is why it has 469 rows against the master's 526 ('526 flames' in the PSI approach is the master row count, not 526 separate ignitions). The table also lacks every measured quantity (flame length, smoke flag) and has no smoke-point column, so it cannot be used alone to reproduce SPICE results.

Other table issues: 25 rows have blank air rate ('Ku LOS', 'no data', or Nikon rows where the formula was not filled); 10 rows have zero hydrocarbon fuel rate (LOS rows and a 'ran out of fuel' row); the 75% propylene label is spelled two ways ('75 % Propylene' 119 rows, '75% Propylene' 16); GMT ignition times use mixed formats (14:37:08, 14.43.58, 1744, 'no ku', 'Ku LOS'); in tests.csv the date column is empty because GMT day-of-year was not converted (all 2009); and fuel_fraction is null for pure fuels and methane.

Max air rate in the table (85.28 cm/s, GMT 052) is above the 65 cm/s maximum at smoke points and the 5-50 cm/s design requirement; it is a single reading during a fan sweep and was not checked further.

Not readable: SPICE SRD (.doc), 'SPICE Overview.ppt', 'SPICE-1 Ops Overview and Smoke Point Cue Card.ppt' (legacy formats, unsupported by the extractor); the assembly drawing PDF has no text layer. The 2011 crew training gives the cue-card text, so the ops procedure is covered. Imagery, picture books and videos (about 6.9 GB) were not downloaded.

The final report's Appendices B-F (the 2009 ESSCI, 2010 AIAA, 33rd Symposium, Leeds and Fire Safety Journal papers) are empty placeholders in PSI. The Fire Safety Journal paper (doi 10.1016/j.firesaf.2011.08.002, listed in the metadata) was not fetched because sections 1-4 already covered the results. The figures (L_SP vs u_a, L_SP vs \dot m_f/Z_st, TSI plot) are images, so per-point values were taken from SmokePointReview-0g-3.xlsx and cited as psi_table.
Personal contact details (emails, phone numbers) appear in the PSI record contacts and the crew-training decks; they were not copied.

Metadata oddities: the ISA metadata zip is named 'PSI-176_SPICE', and its study design descriptors include 'butane-lighter flame', which does not match SPICE. The PSI record has no start/end dates; dates here come from the final report (12 sessions, 14 Feb - 23 Jun 2009).
Per-run O2, pressure and temperature were not logged in PSI for SPICE; only the 19-24% O2 cabin range is stated.
